title: Content optimization: 20 tactics to boost SEO & AI visibility
summary: Content optimization makes your pages work for readers, search, and AI at once. Get 20 tactics to boost visibility and conversions.
body_text: Content optimization improves existing content so it stays useful, findable, and persuasive after publication. Most advice treats optimizing for readers and optimizing for algorithms as a trade-off. It isn’t. The things that make a page useful to a reader (clear answers, complete coverage, credible sources, strong structure) also help search engines classify it and AI systems cite it. This guide covers 20 tactics for doing that work, grouped by reader, search, and AI needs so you can find the specific weakness on a page. Strong content doesn't choose between readers and algorithms Content that works well for readers often gives search engines and AI systems the same things they need: clear answers, complete coverage, credible support, and strong structure. For example, a direct answer at the start of a section helps readers understand the point quickly. It also helps search engines identify what the section covers and gives AI systems a self-contained passage they can retrieve and summarize. The same principle applies across the page. Clear headings make content easier to scan and interpret. Credible sources help readers trust the information while giving search engines and AI systems clearer attribution and context. So reader-first, search-friendly, and AI-ready optimization are not separate workflows. Rankings and citations follow when content is useful, clear, well-supported, and easy to understand. The tactics in this guide are grouped by reader, search, and AI needs so you can identify specific weaknesses on a page. But many improvements support all three evaluators at once. What is content optimization? Content optimization is the process of improving existing content so it reaches more people and encourages more of them to act. Today, that means making a page work for three evaluators: readers, search engines, and AI systems, so it can earn more visibility, trust, and conversions. For example, you might optimize a blog post so it ranks higher in Google, appears in AI-generated answers, or encourages more people to sign up, book a demo, or make a purchase. Content optimization can include: Updating outdated facts, examples, and screenshots Adding missing subtopics or common questions Adding expert insights, data, or credible sources Making the content easier to understand Improving headings, title tags, and meta descriptions Why is content optimization important? Content optimization is important because it helps published content stay accurate, up to date, and useful enough to drive traffic, leads, signups, or sales. When content becomes outdated, readers may trust it less, search engines may rank it lower for queries that need fresh information, and AI systems may be less likely to cite it in answers. Google has freshness systems designed to show newer content when a query calls for current information. AI systems also appear to favor recent or recently updated pages. A Seer Interactive study found that almost 90% of AI bot activity focused on content published within the past three years, with the strongest preference for pages updated between 2023 and 2025. At Semrush, we regularly optimize our content. For example, our link building guide has been updated several times since publication. And it still ranks on Google’s first page. It appears as a source in Google’s AI Mode. And it shows up in ChatGPT’s web results. How to optimize content for the reader You can optimize your content for readers by making the page useful, clear, and easy to act on. Start with these content optimization tips for improving the reader experience: 1. Match search intent to improve rankings Search intent is the reason someone searches for a keyword. Ensuring your content aligns with search intent helps your page match what the searcher wants to do or learn. There are four main types of search intent: Informational : The user wants to learn about a topic Transactional : The user wants to make a purchase or complete an action Navigational : The user wants to find a specific website or page Commercial : The user wants to compare options before buying To determine search intent, check the top-ranking results for your target keyword. For example, searching for “influencer marketing tools” shows mostly list and comparison posts, which means the keyword has commercial and informational intent. You can also use Semrush’s Keyword Overview tool. Enter your keyword and review the “Intent” field to see whether the keyword is informational, commercial, transactional, navigational, or a mix of these. Once you know the intent, update the page to match it. You may need to change the format, add missing sections, remove irrelevant information, improve examples, update the CTA, or make the answer more direct. The goal is to give readers what they expected to find. Intent alignment can also improve search visibility because Google wants to show relevant content for each query. And when your page clearly answers the query, even AI systems are more likely to summarize or cite it in AI-generated answers. 2. Cover the topic comprehensively Covering a topic comprehensively involves answering the main question and the follow-up questions a reader needs before deciding what to do next. To identify what’s missing in your content and where you can improve, start with a SERP analysis . Use Semrush’s Keyword Overview to review the top-ranking pages for your target keyword to see what they cover. Open the tool, enter your keyword, and then scroll to the “SERP Analysis” section of the report. Visit these top-ranking pages one by one and manually examine their content. Look for specific details like: Missing subtopics : Questions or sections competitors cover that your page does not Content depth : Areas where competing pages explain the topic more clearly or completely Examples : Screenshots, workflows, use cases, or data points that make the content easier to understand Visuals : Images, charts, tables, or videos that help readers understand the topic faster But don’t copy the same structure or repeat the same information. Use the SERP to understand what readers expect. Then add something better and unique, such as a clearer workflow, stronger example, expert insight, original data, etc. Comprehensive coverage also gives search engines more context about the topic and AI systems more relevant passages to retrieve. 3. Make your content easy to understand Easy-to-understand content helps readers find answers faster and stay engaged. Focus on two main things: clear language and clear structure. Clear language makes the answer easier to understand on the first read. For example, this sentence is hard to read: “The optimization of the page should be conducted in a way that allows the user’s query to be addressed.” This version is clearer: “Optimize the page so it answers the user’s question.” Here are a few ways to make your writing clearer: Explain jargon the first time you use it Put the main answer at the start of each section Use active voice where possible Replace long sentences with shorter ones Use specific words instead of vague phrases Cut repeated points or filler sentences Add examples when a concept feels abstract Check out our guide on how to become a better writer . Next, clear structure helps readers skim. It also makes sections easier for search engines to classify and gives AI systems clearer passages to extract. Here are a few ways to structure your content clearly: Use clear H2 and H3 headings Keep paragraphs short Use bullet points for lists Add a table of contents for longer pages Use tables when comparing options Add visuals when they make an idea easier to understand Group related points under the same section 4. Keep content fresh to sustain visibility Refreshing content helps readers trust your page because it keeps the information accurate, current, and useful. Fresh content also gives search engines and AI systems more current information to summarize or cite. Start with important pages, such as product/service pages, high-traffic blog posts, or pages that help generate leads, signups, or sales. Audit them and look for updates you can make, such as: Replace outdated statistics Update old screenshots Add new examples Fix broken links Add internal links to relevant pages Remove outdated advice Update the CTA if the reader’s next step has changed Next, prioritize pages that are starting to lose visibility. They’ve already shown they can perform. Updating them can help you recover value faster than creating a new page from scratch. You can use Semrush’s Position Tracking tool to find which pages are losing visibility for important keywords across Google, ChatGPT, and Google AI Mode. Open the tool and configure your tracking campaign . Then go to the “ Overview ” report and check the “Rankings Overview” table to see how your pages are performing for each keyword. Look for pages that have dropped in position, disappeared from the results, or been overtaken by a competitor. Then compare them with the current top-ranking results. Check whether your page still matches search intent, answers the main question clearly, covers the topic well, and gives readers a useful next step. Update the page based on what is missing. How to optimize content for search engines You can optimize your content for search engines by making your page easier to crawl, understand, and classify for relevant searches. Here are six ways: 5. Use secondary keywords to expand reach Secondary keywords are related search terms your page can rank for alongside its primary keyword. For example, if your main keyword is “content optimization,” secondary keywords might include “content optimization tools,” “SEO content optimization,” and “content optimization strategy.” Adding secondary keywords shows that your page covers related questions and subtopics around the main keyword. This broader coverage can help your page appear for more searches around the same topic and give AI systems more context to understand, summarize, or cite your content. Use Semrush’s Keyword Magic Tool to find secondary keywords. Open the tool, enter your primary keyword, and click “ Search .” The tool will generate a list of related keywords, along with key metrics for each, such as: Intent : What users want from the query Volume : How many searches the keyword gets monthly Keyword Difficulty (KD %) : How hard it is to rank in the top 10 results To find high-volume terms, set the " Volume " filter to “ 1,000 ” or higher, then click “ Apply .” You’ll see keywords with at least 1,000 monthly searches. Review the list and select the most relevant options. Then include them naturally in headings, introductions, and key sections where they fit contextually. 6. Add semantically related terms Semantically related terms are words and phrases that add context and depth to your main topic, even when they're not separate keywords you’re trying to rank for. These terms help search engines and AI systems understand how the ideas on your page connect. They also help readers because they make the page more complete and useful. You can use Google autocomplete to find semantically related words and angles people search for. For example, if your primary keyword is “how to grow tomatoes,” autocomplete suggestions may include phrases like “in pots,” “from seeds,” “in containers,” and “in a raised bed.” You can also find words semantically related to your primary keyword in Semrush’s Keyword Magic Tool . Go to the “ Related ” tab and review the keyword groups in the left-side panel. Once you have a list of semantic keywords, check whether your page already explains the ideas behind them. In our example, terms like “soil,” “sun,” “seeds,” and “pots” all point to important parts of growing tomatoes. If one of those ideas is missing, add a short section, FAQ, example, image, or step that covers it. If a term does not fit the page, skip it. 7. Improve on-page SEO for better search performance On-page SEO improves search performance by fixing page-level issues that make your content harder to understand, scan, or show in search results. Begin with this simple content optimization SEO checklist for important pages: Title tag : Clearly describe the page and include the primary keyword if it fits naturally Meta description : Summarize the page in a way that encourages users to click H1 : Make the main topic obvious H2s and H3s : Organize the page into clear sections URL slug : Keep it short, readable, and descriptive Internal links : Point readers and search engines to related pages Image alt text : Describe important images clearly For content-heavy pages, focus on making the information easy to navigate and understand at a glance. Break up long sections with clear subheadings, keep paragraphs concise, and make sure each section directly contributes to answering the user’s query. This helps users find what they need faster and makes the page easier for search engines and AI systems to interpret and summarize. You can use Semrush’s Site Audit tool to find content optimization issues at scale. Open the tool, enter your domain, and complete the configuration to run an audit. Then go to the “ Issues ” tab and search for “content optimization.” Review each affected page and check what needs to be improved. After fixing the issues, rerun the audit to check whether they have been resolved. 8. Optimize visual content Optimizing visual content helps search engines interpret your images and videos and can improve page performance. Use these visual optimization tactics: Add descriptive alt text that explains the image clearly Compress image files to improve page speed Use descriptive file names instead of generic names like “image123.jpg” Add captions when an image needs context Add transcripts for videos when they help users and search engines understand the content These changes can also improve accessibility for readers and help AI systems identify what the visual contains. 9. Optimize your page for SERP features Optimizing for SERP features helps your content appear in enhanced search results, not just standard organic listings. SERP features can include AI Overviews , featured snippets , People Also Ask boxes, image packs, video results, review snippets, and local packs . These features can make your content more visible in search results and give users a clearer reason to click. Start by checking which SERP features appear for your target keyword. Open Semrush’s Keyword Overview tool, enter your target keyword, and scroll to the “SERP Analysis” section. Review the SERP features listed for that keyword and click “ View SERP ” to see what the results look like on Google. Then optimize your content for the feature that fits the keyword and your page type. Here are a few best practices: Match the SERP format : If the current results use a paragraph, list, table, or video, structure your content in a similar format when it fits your page Answer the query directly : Give a clear answer near the top of the relevant section before adding examples or extra detail Use question-led headings : Use clear H2s and H3s that reflect the questions users search for Support visual intent : Add useful visuals and optimize the file name, title, caption, and alt text Back up key claims : Use credible sources, examples, or data when the topic requires proof Clear, well-structured answers can also make relevant information easier for AI systems to identify and extract. Read our guide on how to optimize for SERP features to learn how to target specific search features. 10. Optimize for rich results with schema markup Schema markup is code you add to a page to label key details, such as ratings, prices, authors, events, and business information. These details can help your page qualify for rich results, which are enhanced search listings that show extra information in search results beyond the standard title, URL, and description. Like this: Schema markup can also give AI systems cleaner page details to work with when they summarize information from your content. Common schema types include Article for blog posts, Product for product pages, Breadcrumb for site navigation, LocalBusiness for local pages, Event for event pages, and Organization for company details. To add schema markup, use your CMS or SEO plugin, add JSON-LD directly, or ask a developer to implement it. For exact steps, check out our guide on how to add schema markup to your website . Then test the page with Google’s Rich Results Test to check whether Google can read the structured data. And fix any critical errors before publishing. Semrush’s Site Audit tool can help you find schema issues across your site. Go to the “Markup” thematic report in the “Overview” tab. You’ll see a markup score based on valid and invalid structured data items. Review the “Structured Data Items” section to see which items are valid or invalid. Fix invalid items so search engines can read your structured data correctly. How to optimize content for AI systems You can optimize content for AI systems by making each important section easy to retrieve, understand, summarize, and cite. This work is also called generative engine optimization . Here are three ways: 11. Optimize for AI prompts Optimizing for AI prompts involves finding the questions people ask in AI tools and answering them clearly in your content. This can improve AI visibility , as clear, complete answers are more likely to be retrieved, summarized, or cited by AI systems. AI prompts are often more specific than keyword searches. For example, someone might search Google for “organic farming tips.” But in ChatGPT, they might ask, “What are the best organic farming tips for beginners growing vegetables in a small backyard?” To find relevant prompts, start with first-party data. Review sales calls, demo transcripts, support tickets, chat logs, customer surveys, and on-site search data. Look for repeated questions, objections, use cases, and comparison points. You can also use Semrush’s Prompt Research to find prompts at scale. Open the tool, enter a topic related to your brand, product, or page, and click “ Analyze .” In the “Related topics” section, review topic clusters by volume, relevance, and intent. Open the most relevant topic clusters to review the individual prompts inside them. Choose prompts that are directly relevant to the page and can be answered without going off-topic. If a prompt fits an existing page, add it as a section, FAQ, comparison point, or example. If the prompt needs a deeper answer, create a new page around it. 12. Use structured comparison tables to earn AI citations Structured comparison tables make important details easier for AI systems to extract, compare, summarize, and cite. They also help readers compare options quickly. To make comparison tables useful: Use clear column names Compare the same criteria for every option Keep each cell short and specific Include only details that help the reader decide Add a short takeaway after the table Update the table when features, pricing, or recommendations change 13. Build entity clarity into your content Entity clarity means naming the specific brands, tools, people, products, and concepts your content refers to. Clear names help AI systems connect your content to the right subject, source, and context. Vague references make that harder. Specific naming also makes the content clearer for readers and gives search engines better context about the entities discussed. Before publishing, check that you: Name tools, products, brands, and reports specifically Use the same term for the same concept throughout the page Link author and contributor bios when expertise affects trust Keep claims close to the source, data, or example that supports them For example, don’t write: “The device can help you monitor your health.” Write: “Apple Watch Series 11 can track your heart rate and sleep duration.” The clearer version names the device, the action, and the specific metrics being tracked. Further reading : How to Optimize Content for AI Search Engines [2026 Guide] How to optimize content for higher credibility Credible content gives readers, search engines, and AI systems stronger reasons to trust your page, which helps improve visibility, engagement, and the likelihood of being cited or recommended. Here are four ways to build credibility into your existing content: 14. Include author and contributor bios Author and contributor bios show who created or reviewed the content and why they’re qualified to cover the topic. Include details such as the person’s name, role, area of expertise, relevant experience, and links to their author page or professional profile. For example, Semrush author pages show who wrote the article and provide more context about the author’s expertise. Named authors with linked bios also help AI systems identify the entity behind the content, which supports trust when they choose sources to cite. 15. Include expert insight Including expert insight makes content more credible when the topic needs experience, judgment, or technical accuracy. It helps readers trust your content more and gives search engines and AI systems more evidence that the content is supported by real expertise. Interview subject matter experts or include them in the review process. Use their input to add practical warnings, common mistakes, real examples, trade-offs, or firsthand advice. Here’s an example of an expert quote in a Semrush article: 16. Include original research Original research gives readers unique evidence, gives publishers something worth linking to, and gives AI systems a source they can cite. For example, Semrush's study " Does AI content rank well in search ?" includes original research and has earned more than 1,800 backlinks. It’s also cited by multiple AI tools. Here are a few ways to create original research: Surveys : Collect insights through Google Forms or SurveyMonkey Interviews : Speak with customers, experts, or employees Case studies : Share examples of customer success or problem-solving Platform analytics : Analyze your own data to uncover trends 17. Use credible sources Credible sources make your claims easier for readers to verify and give search engines and AI systems clearer attribution. Different claims require different types of sources: Rely on official documentation for product, platform, or policy claims Reference original studies for statistics Turn to government, academic, or institutional sources when the topic requires stronger proof Place the source close to the claim it supports. Avoid weak sources for important claims. Further reading : Google E-E-A-T: What it is & how it affects SEO How to optimize your content for conversions Conversion optimization turns the visibility and trust your content earns into business results, such as signups, demo requests, purchases, or contact form submissions. Here are three ways to optimize your content for conversion: 18. Demonstrate the value of your product or service Showing your product or service in action helps readers understand how it solves their problems. When readers see clear, relevant use cases, they’re more likely to convert. For example, you’ll notice many Semrush blog posts include workflows that demonstrate how to use Semrush tools to achieve specific goals. Like this one showing readers how to find buyer intent keywords using the free keyword tool . However, avoid forcing product mentions. Only include them where they naturally fit and genuinely help readers achieve their goals. Demonstrating real, practical value builds trust and keeps your content persuasive without sounding promotional. 19. Add social proof to build trust Social proof (such as testimonials, case studies, and success stories) shows potential customers that others have benefited from your product or service. It builds credibility and can make readers more confident about taking the next step. For example, in a post about influencer marketing campaigns, you could feature a short case study showing how a brand used your influencer search software, followed by a direct customer testimonial. A clear, authentic customer quote adds weight and emotional trust. Insider One uses this approach effectively. The company includes five-star reviews in its content to address a key audience challenge (MarTech implementation) and reassure readers that its solution delivers results. Reviews and testimonials can also give AI systems more third-party context when describing or comparing a brand. 20. Use calls to action that fit the reader’s journey A call to action (CTA) tells readers what to do next. Clear CTAs increase engagement and guide users toward conversion, such as signing up, contacting your team, or making a purchase. Common CTAs include: Sign Up Now Contact Us Buy Now The key is to match the CTA with the reader’s stage in the journey. For example, this CTA on the Semrush blog uses the CTA “Sign up now,” along with text that explains the benefits of signing up to try Traffic & Market Toolkit . A CTA should: Be specific and action-oriented Explain the benefit of clicking Fit the user’s intent and content context Relevant, well-placed CTAs help turn the visibility and trust your content earns into signups, leads, or sales without interrupting the reading experience. How to measure content optimization results You can measure content optimization results by comparing how a page performs before and after you update it. This helps you see whether your changes improved reader engagement, search visibility, AI visibility, or conversions. The exact metrics to track depend on the page’s main job. For instance, a blog post may need to earn search traffic, answer AI prompts, and drive newsletter signups. A product page may need to rank for commercial keywords, build trust, and drive purchases or demo requests. Once you know the page’s job, review how it performs with readers, in search results, and across AI systems. Together, these signals show whether the page is earning engagement, visibility, and business results. Area Signals to track What it tells you Tools to use Readers Time on page, scroll depth, CTA clicks, signups, demo requests, purchases, or form submissions Whether readers engage with the page and take the next step Google Analytics , your CRM, or your analytics platform Search Clicks, impressions, CTR, average position, keyword rankings, organic traffic, and unresolved site issues Whether the page is visible, clickable, and technically healthy in search Google Search Console , Position Tracking , and Site Audit AI visibility Brand mentions , citations, share of voice, sentiment, prompt visibility Whether AI systems find, reference, and describe your content accurately AI Visibility Toolkit Track the same signals after each major update to see whether the page performs better across all three areas. If a page is underperforming in AI answers specifically, here's how to find your AI visibility gaps . Frequently asked questions How is optimizing for AI search different from SEO? SEO focuses mainly on helping pages rank for relevant searches, while AI optimization places more emphasis on making specific passages easy to retrieve, summarize, and cite. The two approaches still overlap. Clear answers, strong structure, accurate information, credible sources, and specific entity names can support both search rankings and AI visibility. What’s the difference between content optimization and content creation? Content creation involves producing a new page or asset, while content optimization involves improving something that already exists. For example, creating a new guide is content creation. Updating its statistics, adding missing sections, improving its headings, and strengthening its CTA are content optimization. How do you optimize content for Perplexity and ChatGPT specifically? You can optimize content for Perplexity and ChatGPT by publishing accurate, current pages with clear answers, descriptive headings, specific entity names, and credible sources. You should also allow OAI-SearchBot and PerplexityBot to access your site so both platforms can discover and surface your content in search results. How often should you optimize existing content? You should optimize existing content whenever it becomes outdated, loses visibility, stops converting, or no longer matches what readers need. Review high-value and fast-changing pages more frequently, and update them as soon as important facts, screenshots, products, rankings, or user expectations change. What tools should you use for content optimization? You should use tools that help you find content gaps and improve the page, such as keyword and SERP research tools, prompt research tools, content optimization editors, readability tools, and site audit tools. Choose each tool based on the issue you need to fix, such as missing subtopics, unclear writing, weak structure, or technical problems. Start by optimizing one important page today One of the easiest ways to start content optimization is to choose an important page and run it through Semrush’s Content Optimizer . Open the tool, choose “ Optimize existing article ,” enter the page URL or paste your content, and click “ Optimize article .” The tool reviews your page for SEO, AI search visibility, readability, structure, clarity, and engagement. It shows suggestions to make the page clearer, more useful, and easier to find. Try Content Optimizer today. title: Building Burstables: cpu slicing with cgroups
summary: Burstable VMs run on a fraction of CPU and burst to a higher level of CPU usage to support occasional usage spikes. To implement them, we leveraged Control Groups v2 (cgroups v2), a Linux kernel feature that helps manage resource usage. We thought our open-source implementation of burstable VMs might be interesting enough to write about. We also learned a lot about Linux cgroups in the process!
body_text: Building Burstables: cpu slicing with cgroups April 29, 2025 · 6 min read Maciek Sarnowicz Contributor Ubicloud is an open source alternative to AWS. You can self-host our software or use our managed service to reduce your cloud costs by 3x. ‍ Some of our customers told us that the price of dedicated VMs was too steep and asked for a lower entry point. We looked into it and came up with burstable VMs . These VMs run on a fraction of a shared CPU and burst to a higher level of CPU usage to support occasional spikes in usage. To implement burstable VMs, we leveraged Linux Control Groups v2 (cgroups v2), a Linux kernel feature that helps manage resource usage. We thought our open-source implementation of burstable VMs might be interesting enough to write about. We also learned a lot about Linux cgroups in the process! The building blocks Linux cgroups are organized hierarchically. Each group acts as a “container” that can host child groups, processes, and threads. These groups control specific system usage, such as cpu, io, memory, hugetlb, pids, and rdma. You can also configure cpusets to control the cpu and memory placement of Linux processes. At each group level, you can enable specific controllers to set resource limits. These resource limits apply to the group’s children (other groups and processes) and also make that controller available to the children’s groups. For example, if we enable the memory controller for a group called "webservices", we can set a memory limit of 4GB for this group. Then, any processes within this group will share this 4GB allocation. We could further create child groups like "webservices/frontend" with 1.5GB and "webservices/backend" with 2.5GB, distributing the parent's resources among children. You can use cgroups either through the virtual filesystem or through Linux’s system manager (systemd). However, not all of cgroup’s functionality is exposed through systemd. In particular, the CPU burst settings are not. Cgroups through a virtual filesystem You can inspect the Control Group hierarchy and configuration through a virtual filesystem mounted at /sys/fs/cgroup . Key files include: cgroup.controllers: Lists all available controllers cgroup.subtree_control: Defines controllers selected for this cgroup and its descendants cpuset.*: Configuration files for the cpuset controller cpu.*: Configuration files for the CPU controller Most of these files are writable, allowing you to modify configuration settings as needed. Cgroups through systemd In the systemd world, control groups manifest as slices - logical units for managing system resources. By default, systemd already organizes processes into predefined slices like system.slice and user.slice , creating a natural hierarchy. We can extend this organization by creating our own custom slice for resource management. For instance, imagine we want to isolate and control resources for a CPU-intensive workload: Our slice definition is remarkably simple: # /etc/systemd/system/example.slice [S lice ] The service that will live within our slice: # /etc/systemd/system/stress.service [S ervice ] Slice=example.slice ExecStart=stress-ng --cpu 1 --cpu-load 50 --cpu-load-slice 100 After starting this service, systemd automatically incorporates our new slice into the hierarchy: CGroup: / ├─example.slice │ └─stress.service │ ├─ 1886 stress-ng --cpu 1 --cpu-load 50 --cpu-load-slice 100 │ └─ 1887 "stress-ng-cpu [run]" ├─system.slice │ ├─cron.service │ │ └─ 637 /usr/sbin/cron -f -P ... └─user.slice └─user- 1000. slice ├─session- 1. scope │ ├─ 724 "sshd: ubi [priv]" ... What makes this approach powerful is how it provides fine-grained control over resource allocation. Each slice becomes a container for managing multiple related processes as a cohesive unit. This organization isn't just visual - it provides a framework for applying resource controls. Our custom example.slice has now become a management point where we can apply specific resource constraints using the various cgroup controllers. The ins and outs of the controllers We utilize two controllers to manage the CPU limits and enable VM instances to burst beyond their allocated limit: cpuset and cpu. ‍ The cpuset controller enables setting a range of CPUs the group can use. Additionally, setting the partition type to root creates an isolated cpu set dedicated to the group and other subgroups and processes. This allows us to create a resource “box” to host a single dedicated VM or a set of burstable VMs sharing the CPUs and to keep those VMs from running workloads on CPUs belonging to other groups. ‍ The cpu controller allows setting the maximum CPU limit ( cpu.max ), which controls the amount of the host’s CPU allocated to individual VMs. When we put multiple VMs inside one group, we can restrict their CPU allocation at each VM level to control the amount of CPU sharing in the group. Furthermore, we can set the cpu.max.burst limit for each VM to allow it to occasionally exceed the regular CPU limit. The burstability controls were first implemented in the Linux kernel by Alibaba engineer Huaixin Chang ( source ) and further evolved with the cgroups v2 implementation. The kernel controls the amount of bursting and awards the CPU “credits” accumulated over time by a process up to a specific limit. For example, if the process’s maximum CPU limit is set to 100%, the burst limit is set at an additional 100%, and the process has been running at an average of 70%, it accumulates a 30% CPU credit that allows it to burst up to 130%. This is all, of course, also constrained by time. The credits are accumulated and dispensed at CPU scheduling intervals, which are sub-second. With our example.slice in place, we can now leverage the cgroup filesystem interface to apply resource constraints. Let's check the current CPU allocation: $ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/example.slice/cpu.max max 100000 The output indicates our slice currently has unlimited CPU access (shown by "max") within the standard quota period of 100,000 microseconds. We can easily throttle the CPU usage by modifying this file: $ echo "25000 100000" | sudo tee / sys / fs / cgroup / example.slice / cpu.max With this change, we've allocated only 25% of CPU resources to everything in our example.slice - including our stress-testing service. The running stress-ng process is immediately affected, now limited to using at most a quarter of the available CPU resources.To see the effect of our changes, we can examine the CPU statistics: $ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/example.slice/cpu.stat This reveals real-time metrics on CPU usage, throttling events, and burst utilization - showing exactly how our constraints are being enforced on the workload. Putting it all together Combining all of the above, here is how we now control virtual machines on a host: We create slice units and assign a set of dedicated host CPUs to each of them. The Standard VMs run each in their own cgroup (slice), with an isolated set of host CPUs assigned. We create those on-demand with each VM, and their lifespan is tied together. The Burstable VMs are placed in a cgroup where instances share a set of host CPUs. We place the new instances in an existing slice unit or create a new slice if needed. Each VM is provided with a minimum CPU allocation at 50% of the vCPU limit and can burst into the shared space at up to 100% of the vCPU limit. Because the CPU is shared, the ability to burst is not guaranteed. At the same time, the burstable instances are confined within their own group and cannot interfere with Standard VMs running on the same host. We can inspect the configuration of each cgroup (slice) by inspecting the content of virtual files stored at each cgroup’s unit level under /system/fs/cgroup/<cgroup-name> . Here is an example from our implementation: cgroup.controllers: cpuset cpu memory pids cgroup.subtree_control: cpu memory pids cpuset.cpus: 4 - 5 cpuset.cpus.effective: 4 - 5 cpuset.cpus.partition: root cpu.max: max 100000 cpu.max.burst: 0 All this functionality is orchestrated by our control plane. It tracks the CPU allocation to each cgroup and each VM, calculates the limits, and assigns them based on the VM size and its specification mapped to the host’s architecture. Some cgroup settings are not preserved over host restarts, therefore, we ensure that the control plane re-applies them as needed and when needed. Also, we paid attention to the VM provisioning time and ensured that all this new functionality did not increase it. We made the cgroup setup logic run in parallel to other tasks performed during the provisioning of a VM and kept the overall elapsed time unchanged. Performance Testing – CPU-bound workload We ran a simple stress test simulating a CPU-bound and bursty workload to see how the burstability is used. For this, we used the stress-ng utility. stress-ng --cpu 2 --cpu-load 60 --cpu-load-slice 100 --timeout 60 s We run stress-ng on the following set of servers: A standard-2 instance to observe how it behaves on a relatively “unconstrained” instance. Note that the workload doesn’t fully use the standard-2 instance A single burstable-2 instance, representing a low-density scenario where no other workloads are running on the neighboring instances Multiple burstable-2 instances, representing a high-density scenario where all instances sharing a set of CPUs are equally loaded similar single-instance and multiple instances runs for burstable-1 VMs. The workload is sized such that it utilizes close to the full capacity of the burstable instances, but because it is not a constant load, it allows for some effects of burstability. We can observe the following: When burstable-2 instances run without much neighboring workload, they can utilize the burstability as they have room to expand. We observe about 30% improvement for this workload. Conversely, when all instances in a shared CPU set are fully loaded, there is no room for bursting, and the VMs cannot achieve the same results. When the workload is too large for the instance’s size, such as when we run the 2-cpu workload on a burstable-1 instance, there is no room to accumulate bursting credits. As a result, we don’t use the bursting capability (last two columns on the chart). We then run a 1-cpu workload only on burstable-1 instances: stress-ng --cpu 1 --cpu-load 60 --cpu-load-slice 100 --timeout 60 s Here we can see that when the workload is sized correctly to the server size, and there are no neighboring instances taking away the shared CPU, the workload has room to burst into and improves by about 30%. Next up Quick Start - Build your own cloud Takeaways We have four takeaways from building burstables. First, burstable VMs provide a cost-effective solution for workloads that can run on a fraction of a vCPU. Examples include small websites, SaaS services, development and test environments. For example, a simple fault-tolerant web app requires at least two VMs behind a load balancer, backed by a managed Postgres database. The total cost of that setup with dedicated 8GB instances was $100/month ($0.14/hr) on Ubicloud before the introduction of burstable VMs. With burstable instances, the cost drops to less than $25/month ($0.035/hr). Second, our experiments show that once the burstable instance is correctly sized to the workload, you get about 30% burst capacity during resource spikes. Third, sadly, cgroups v2 restricts this burst capacity to micro-intervals - and the burst credits don’t accumulate over minutes or hours. Aggregating and applying burst credits over a longer time period requires that we collect statistics and apply burst credits outside of the cgroups v2 implementation. We haven’t yet incorporated these changes into our implementation. Finally, even with this small caveat, we found cgroups v2 to provide robust resource management across VMs. VMs exceed their baseline allocation when needed, while maintaining strong isolation between workload groups. Linux and open source virtualization solutions have come a long way since the early days of the cloud . As we improve our open source cloud, we’re committed to transparently sharing our implementation details. If you have any questions or comments, please drop us a line at [email protected] anytime.

title: Advanced AI and Machine Vision Build Resilient Supply Chains
summary: Manufacturing and logistics leaders face a complex, shifting landscape. The relentless pace of e-commerce, persistent labor shortages, and rising consumer expectations demand a new approach to operational strategy.
body_text: Manufacturing and logistics leaders face a complex, shifting landscape. The relentless pace of e-commerce, persistent labor shortages, and rising consumer expectations demand a new approach to operational strategy. Companies that embrace intelligent automation and digitize their frontline operations find themselves better equipped to navigate these challenges and build resilient, efficient, and profitable businesses. The path forward requires a deep understanding of the trends shaping our industries and the technologies capable of addressing our most significant pain points. The Automation Imperative Across the supply chain, from the factory floor to the warehouse dock, automation answers the critical challenge of workforce attrition. Intelligent factories leverage advanced tools to fill labor gaps, enhance productivity, and empower workers. Technologies like autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) and AI-driven decision-making tools reduce the reliance on manual labor for repetitive tasks. This shift allows employees to focus on higher-value activities like quality assurance and customer service. Smart warehouses, powered by the Internet of Things (IoT) and robotics, create adaptable, autonomous systems that respond dynamically to operational changes, ensuring that smaller, faster orders reach consumers with precision. Harnessing Data for Intelligent Action The modern operational environment generates a tremendous amount of data. Our ability to capture, analyze, and act upon this information in real time defines our competitive advantage. The convergence of Information Technology and Operational Technology (IT/OT) drives efficiency through combinatorial innovation. AI tools, machine vision, and RFID are increasingly integrated to optimize processes. These solutions provide the asset visibility and connected collaboration necessary for intelligent operations . For example, machine vision systems equipped with on-device AI can identify product defects during production, allowing for immediate corrective action. This real-time quality control minimizes waste and improves output. RFID provides an always-on stream of data, offering unparalleled insight into inventory levels and movement throughout the supply chain. Building a Resilient, Customer-Focused Future Operational resilience now stands as a primary business objective. Investments in intelligent automation provide flexibility to scale operations and maintain continuity during periods of disruption. This capability directly enhances the consumer experience, ensuring the speed and accuracy that modern shoppers demand. Technologies like AI-powered warehouse execution systems (WES) streamline workflows to meet the growing demand for seamless shopping experiences. We design our entire portfolio of hardware, software, and automation solutions with this vision in mind. We relentlessly pursue innovation, focusing on customer commitment and a leading partner ecosystem to help organizations digitize, automate, and optimize their frontline operations. We believe this work makes everyday life better for our customers, their employees, and the people they serve. At MODEX 2026, I had the pleasure of discussing these very topics with my colleague Ritesh Gupta , Director of Application Engineering at Zebra. We explored how customers use our technologies, from AI-enabled cameras that prevent conveyor jams to 3D vision solutions that enable dimensioning in motion, to solve their toughest challenges. I invite you to watch our full conversation and see how the right combination of technologies can help you achieve real-time insight, enable connected collaboration, and create optimized workflows to give your business its ultimate edge. Watch our full Linkedln Live session here .
